A: Chapter 10 is the Lord's account of his manifestations (vibhūti), given, as he says, out of a wish for Arjuna's welfare (10.1). Movements: (1) 10.1–11 — the Lord announces his supreme word; neither gods nor great seers know his origin, since he is their beginning (10.2); whoever knows him as unborn, beginningless lord of the world is undeluded and freed from sins (10.3); all the states of beings, and the seven great seers and the Manus, come from him (10.4–6); knowing his vibhūti and yoga brings unwavering yoga (10.7); knowing him as the origin of all, the wise worship him with their thought on him, speaking of him to one another (10.8–9), and to these he gives the yoga of understanding and destroys the darkness born of ignorance (10.10–11). (2) 10.12–18 — Arjuna acknowledges him as the supreme brahman and eternal Person, as the seers (Nārada, Asita Devala, Vyāsa) proclaim (10.12–13); only he knows himself by himself (10.15); Arjuna asks to be told his manifestations and in which things he is to be contemplated (10.16–18). (3) 10.19–39 — the Lord names his principal manifestations: first the self seated in all beings and the beginning, middle and end of beings (10.20), then the chief of each class of gods, seers, beings, things, sounds, times and qualities (10.21–38), and finally the seed of all beings without which nothing exists (10.39). (4) 10.40–42 — there is no end to his manifestations; whatever is glorious or mighty springs from a portion of his splendour; he stands supporting the whole world with a single portion. Purpose as the chapter states it: that Arjuna may know the Lord and contemplate him in all excellent things (10.17, 10.41).
B: Chapter 10 (vibhūti). Movements: (1) 10.1–11 — the Lord resumes his supreme word for Arjuna's good: neither gods nor seers know his origin, since he is their origin (10.2); knowing him as unborn and beginningless frees from sin (10.3); the states of beings arise from him alone (10.4–5); the seers and Manus born of mind share his being (10.6); knowing his vibhūti and yoga in truth joins one to unwavering yoga (10.7); the wise worship him as the source of all, with citta and prāṇa given to him, speaking of him to one another (10.8–9); to them he gives buddhiyoga and, out of compassion, destroys the darkness of ignorance with the lamp of knowledge (10.10–11). (2) 10.12–18 — Arjuna acknowledges him as the supreme brahman, supreme abode and first god, as the seers Nārada, Asita Devala and Vyāsa declared, and asks to hear his self-manifestations in full, so as to know in which things he is to be contemplated (10.17). (3) 10.19–39 — the list of manifestations 'by the chief ones': the self in all beings and their beginning, middle and end (10.20), then the pre-eminent member of class after class — gods, seers, Vedas, the mind among the senses, awareness in beings, the single syllable, japa, time, death, the letter A, silence, knowledge — ending with the Lord as the seed of all beings (10.39). (4) 10.40–42 — there is no end to them; whatever is glorious springs from a portion of his splendour; he stands supporting the whole world with a single portion. Purpose as the chapter states it: that Arjuna, who delights in hearing, may know the Lord's vibhūti and yoga in truth (10.1, 10.7) and have supports for contemplating him (10.17).
resolution: merged: Chapter 10 is the Lord's account of his manifestations (vibhūti), in four movements. (1) 10.1–11: the Lord resumes his supreme word, spoken for Arjuna's welfare because he delights in hearing (10.1); neither the gods nor the great seers know his origin, for he is their beginning (10.2); whoever knows him as unborn, without beginning, the great lord of the world, is undeluded and freed from all sins (10.3); the states of beings, from understanding and knowledge to fame and ill-fame, arise from him alone (10.4–5), and the seven great seers, the four and the Manus, sharing his being, were born of mind, and from them come the world's creatures (10.6); whoever knows this vibhūti and yoga of his in truth is joined with unwavering yoga (10.7); knowing him as the origin of all, the wise worship him, their thought on him, awakening one another and speaking of him, content and delighting (10.8–9); to these, ever yoked and worshipping with love, he gives the yoga of understanding by which they come to him, and out of compassion he destroys their darkness born of ignorance with the lamp of knowledge (10.10–11). (2) 10.12–18: Arjuna acknowledges him as the supreme brahman, the supreme abode, the supreme purifier, the eternal divine Person, as all the seers — Nārada, Asita Devala and Vyāsa — declare and as he himself says (10.12–13); neither gods nor dānavas know his manifestation, and he alone knows himself by himself (10.14–15); Arjuna asks to be told his divine manifestations in full and in which things he is to be contemplated (10.16–18). (3) 10.19–39: the Lord names his manifestations by the principal ones, since there is no end to them (10.19): first the self seated in all beings and the beginning, middle and end of beings (10.20), then the pre-eminent member of class after class — gods, seers, Vedas, the mind among the senses, sentience in beings, the one syllable, japa among sacrifices, time, death, the letter a, silence, knowledge and the rest (10.21–38) — and last the seed of all beings, without which nothing moving or unmoving could exist (10.39). (4) 10.40–42: there is no end to his divine manifestations and this has been only an indication; whatever being is glorious or mighty has arisen from a portion of his splendour; and he stands supporting this whole world with a single portion. Purpose, as the chapter presents it: that Arjuna, who delights in hearing, may know the Lord's vibhūti and yoga in truth (10.1, 10.7) and have supports for contemplating him in all things (10.17, 10.41).

A: Chapter 11 is the vision of the Lord's sovereign, universal form. Movements: (1) 11.1–4 — Arjuna says his delusion is gone through the secret teaching concerning the self, accepts what the Lord has said of himself, and asks, if he is able, to see his sovereign form. (2) 11.5–8 — the Lord bids him behold his manifold divine forms and the whole world standing as one in his body, and, since his own eye cannot see it, gives him a divine eye. (3) 11.9–14 — Sañjaya tells Dhṛtarāṣṭra of the form: many mouths and eyes, divine ornaments and weapons, a light as of a thousand suns, the whole world divided many ways yet standing as one in the god's body; Arjuna, amazed, his hair on end, bows and speaks. (4) 11.15–31 — Arjuna describes what he sees: gods, Brahmā, seers and all beings within the form, without beginning, middle or end; he names it the imperishable, the resting-place of the universe, the guardian of eternal dharma; then the fierce form that makes the worlds and himself tremble, into whose mouths the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Karṇa and warriors of both sides rush like rivers into the sea and moths into a flame; he asks who this fierce one is. (5) 11.32–34 — the Lord answers: 'I am Time, grown mighty, destroyer of worlds'; the warriors will perish even without Arjuna; they are already slain by him; Arjuna is to be merely the instrument, and fight. (6) 11.35–46 — trembling, Arjuna praises him as greater than all, the imperishable, being and non-being and what is beyond, the first god, pervading all and therefore all; he asks forgiveness for past familiarity and asks to see again the crowned, four-armed form. (7) 11.47–51 — the Lord says he showed this form by his own yoga, out of grace, and that it cannot be seen by Vedas, sacrifice, study, gifts, rites or austerity; he tells Arjuna not to fear, resumes his gentle form, and Arjuna is restored. (8) 11.52–55 — the form is hard to see even for gods; only by undivided devotion can the Lord be known, seen and entered in truth; whoever does his work, holds him supreme, is devoted, unattached and without enmity toward any being comes to him.
B: Chapter 11 (the vision of the universal form). Movements: (1) 11.1–4 — Arjuna says his delusion is gone through the teaching and asks, if possible, to see the Lord's sovereign form. (2) 11.5–8 — the Lord bids him behold his countless forms and the whole world standing as one in his body, and gives him a divine eye, since it cannot be seen with ordinary sight. (3) 11.9–14 — Sañjaya tells Dhṛtarāṣṭra of the form shown: many mouths and eyes, divine ornaments and weapons, a radiance like a thousand suns, the world standing as one in the god's body; Arjuna, amazed and with hair on end, bows. (4) 11.15–31 — Arjuna's account of what he sees: the gods and beings within the form; a form without beginning, middle or end; the imperishable, the resting-place of the universe (11.18); the worlds trembling; the warriors of both sides rushing into its mouths like rivers to the sea and moths to the flame; he asks who this fierce one is. (5) 11.32–34 — the Lord answers that he is Time, destroyer of worlds; the warriors are already slain by him; Arjuna is to be merely the instrument and fight. (6) 11.35–46 — trembling, Arjuna praises him (11.36–40), asks forgiveness for past familiarity (11.41–44), and, thrilled and afraid, asks to see the former four-armed form. (7) 11.47–51 — the Lord says the form was shown by his grace and his own yoga and is not attainable by Vedas, sacrifice, study, gifts, rites or austerity; he bids Arjuna not fear, resumes his gentle form, and Arjuna regains composure. (8) 11.52–55 — the form is rare even for gods; by undivided devotion alone can he be known, seen in truth and entered; the one who does his work, holds him highest, is devoted, unattached and without enmity comes to him. Purpose as the chapter presents it: to grant the sight Arjuna asked for (11.3–4), to reveal the Lord as Time directing the battle (11.32–34), and to state the means by which he is seen and reached (11.54–55).
resolution: merged: Chapter 11 is the vision of the Lord's sovereign, universal form, in eight movements. (1) 11.1–4: Arjuna says his delusion is gone through the supreme secret called adhyātma spoken out of favour to him, and that he has heard in detail of the arising and passing of beings and of the Lord's imperishable greatness; he accepts what the Lord has said of himself and asks, if the Lord thinks him able, to see his sovereign form. (2) 11.5–8: the Lord bids him behold his manifold divine forms by hundreds and thousands, the gods and many wonders, and the whole world standing as one in his body; since Arjuna cannot see him with his own eye, he gives him a divine eye to behold his sovereign yoga. (3) 11.9–14: Sañjaya tells Dhṛtarāṣṭra of the form Hari showed: many mouths and eyes, divine ornaments, garlands and raised weapons, facing every way, its light like a thousand suns risen at once; the whole world, divided in many ways, standing as one in the body of the god of gods; Arjuna, amazed, his hair on end, bows and speaks. (4) 11.15–31: Arjuna describes what he sees — the gods, Brahmā, the seers and all hosts of beings in the form; no end, middle or beginning; the imperishable, the supreme to be known, the resting-place of the universe, the guardian of eternal dharma; then the fierce form at which the worlds and he himself are shaken, into whose flaming mouths the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Bhīṣma, Droṇa, Karṇa and the warriors of his own side rush like rivers into the ocean and moths into a flame — and asks who this fierce one is. (5) 11.32–34: the Lord answers: 'I am Time, grown mighty, maker of the destruction of the worlds'; even without Arjuna the warriors will cease to be; they are already slain by him; Arjuna is to rise, be merely the instrument, and fight. (6) 11.35–46: trembling, Arjuna bows and praises him (11.36–40) — greater than all, the imperishable, being and non-being and what is beyond, the first god, pervading all and therefore all — asks forgiveness for past familiarity (11.41–44), and, thrilled and afraid, asks to see again the crowned, four-armed form (11.45–46). (7) 11.47–51: the Lord says he showed this form, never seen before by another, out of grace and by his own yoga, and that it cannot be seen by Vedas, sacrifice, study, gifts, rites or austerities; he bids Arjuna not fear, shows again his own gentle form, and Arjuna is restored to himself. (8) 11.52–55: the form is hard to see, even the gods long to see it; not by Vedas, austerity, giving or sacrifice, but by undivided devotion alone can the Lord be known, seen in truth and entered; whoever does his work, holds him supreme, is devoted, unattached and without enmity toward any being comes to him. Purpose, as the chapter presents it: to grant the sight Arjuna asked for (11.3–4), to reveal the Lord as Time who has already decided the battle (11.32–34), and to state the means by which he is seen and reached (11.54–55).

A: Chapter 12 answers which worshippers know yoga best and lays out the practice of devotion. Movements: (1) 12.1 — Arjuna asks: of those devotees who, ever yoked, worship the Lord, and those who worship the imperishable, the unmanifest, which know yoga best? (2) 12.2–7 — the Lord answers that those who fix their mind on him and worship him with supreme faith are the most yoked; those who worship the indefinable, unmanifest, unthinkable imperishable, restraining the senses, even in understanding everywhere, delighting in the welfare of all beings, also reach him, but their hardship is greater, for the unmanifest goal is hard for the embodied; those who lay down all actions in him and meditate on him with undivided yoga he soon lifts from the ocean of death and saṃsāra. (3) 12.8–12 — graded instruction: fix mind and understanding on him; if the thought cannot be held steady, seek him by the yoga of practice; if incapable of practice, be intent on work for him; if unable even that, give up the fruit of all actions; then a ranking — knowledge above practice, meditation above knowledge, relinquishing the fruit above meditation, with peace following on relinquishment. (4) 12.13–19 — the marks of the devotee dear to him: without hatred, friendly and compassionate, free of 'mine' and 'I', the same in pleasure and pain, content, self-restrained, neither disturbing nor disturbed by the world, free of elation, intolerance, fear and agitation, without expectation, relinquishing undertakings and both good and evil, the same toward friend and foe, honour and dishonour, praise and blame, silent, homeless, steady in judgement, full of devotion; each group ends with the refrain 'he is dear to me'. (5) 12.20 — those who with faith attend to this nectar of dharma, holding him supreme, are exceedingly dear to him.
B: Chapter 12 (devotion). Movements: (1) 12.1 — Arjuna asks which are the better knowers of yoga: the devotees ever joined who worship Kṛṣṇa as just described (11.55), or those who worship the imperishable unmanifest. (2) 12.2–5 — the Lord's answer: those who fix their manas on him and worship him with supreme faith are held the most joined; those who worship the imperishable — indefinable, unmanifest, all-pervading, unthinkable, unchanging — with senses restrained, even-minded and delighting in the welfare of all beings, also reach him; but the hardship is greater for them, since the unmanifest goal is reached with pain by the embodied. (3) 12.6–7 — those who renounce all actions in him and meditate on him with undivided yoga he lifts before long from the ocean of death and saṃsāra. (4) 12.8–12 — a conditional sequence: fix manas and buddhi on him; if unable, seek him by the yoga of practice; if unable, be intent on work for him; if unable, relinquish the fruit of all actions; followed by the ranking of knowledge over practice, meditation over knowledge, relinquishment over meditation, and peace immediately from relinquishment. (5) 12.13–19 — the marks of the devotee dear to the Lord: without hatred, friendly and compassionate, without 'mine' and 'I', even in pleasure and pain, content, restrained, neither troubling nor troubled by the world, free of elation, impatience, fear and agitation, without expectation, the same to friend and foe, in honour and dishonour, praise and blame, silent, homeless, steady, full of devotion — each group closing with 'he is dear to me'. (6) 12.20 — those who with faith follow this nectar of dharma, holding him highest, are exceedingly dear. Purpose as the chapter presents it: to answer which worshippers are the best knowers of yoga (12.1–2) and to lay out graded means and the marks of the devotee (12.8–20).
resolution: merged: Chapter 12 answers which worshippers know yoga best and sets out the practice of devotion, in six movements. (1) 12.1: Arjuna asks which know yoga best — the devotees who, ever yoked in the way just described (11.55), worship the Lord, or those who worship the imperishable, the unmanifest. (2) 12.2–5: the Lord answers that those who fix the mind on him and worship him, ever yoked, with supreme faith, he holds to be the most yoked; those who worship the imperishable — indefinable, unmanifest, all-pervading, unthinkable, unchanging, immovable, constant — restraining the senses, even in understanding everywhere and delighting in the welfare of all beings, also reach him; but their hardship is greater, for the unmanifest goal is reached with difficulty by the embodied. (3) 12.6–7: those who resign all actions to him and, holding him supreme, worship him meditating with undivided yoga, he before long delivers from the ocean of death and saṃsāra. (4) 12.8–12: graded instruction — fix mind and understanding on him alone and you will dwell in him; if the thought cannot be held steady, seek him by the yoga of practice; if unable even to practise, be intent on work for him; if unable even that, taking refuge in his yoga and self-restrained, give up the fruit of all actions; then a ranking — knowledge better than practice, meditation superior to knowledge, relinquishing the fruit of actions superior to meditation, peace following immediately on relinquishment. (5) 12.13–19: the marks of the devotee dear to the Lord — hating no being, friendly and compassionate, without 'mine' and 'I', the same in pain and pleasure, forbearing, content, self-restrained, firm in resolve, mind and understanding offered to him; neither disturbing nor disturbed by the world, free of elation, intolerance, fear and agitation; without expectation, pure, capable, impartial, relinquishing every undertaking; neither rejoicing nor hating, grieving nor craving, having given up good and bad; the same toward enemy and friend, in honour and dishonour, cold and heat, blame and praise; silent, content with whatever comes, homeless, steady in judgement, full of devotion — each group closing with 'he is dear to me'. (6) 12.20: those who with faith, holding him supreme, attend to this nectar of dharma as spoken, are exceedingly dear to him. Purpose, as the chapter presents it: to answer which worshippers are the best knowers of yoga (12.1–2) and to lay out graded means and the marks of the devotee (12.8–20).
